opus-5.5.text:
Oh, dominoes. That was one of those projects that looked simple and turned out not to be.

When you watch dominoes fall in real life, it seems trivial: one tips over, hits the next, and the chain keeps going. So I thought, okay, a few boxes, some gravity, collision detection, done. But once you actually try to simulate it, you run into almost every hard problem in rigid-body dynamics at once.

The first lesson was about **contact**. Dominoes aren't really "colliding" in the clean billiard-ball sense. Most of the time they're resting on the ground, leaning on each other, sliding a little. That persistent, many-body contact is where naive approaches fall apart. If you just detect penetration and push objects apart with a penalty force, you get jitter, objects slowly sinking into each other, or the whole chain exploding when the stiffness is wrong. It made me appreciate why people moved toward constraint-based formulations and complementarity problems instead of just springs.

The second lesson was about **time stepping and stability**. A domino chain is a system where small errors accumulate. If your integrator adds even a tiny bit of energy each step, by the hundredth domino something ridiculous happens. If it removes too much, the chain just stops halfway. So you're always balancing accuracy, stability, and cost. That's when I really started caring about how the numerical method itself shapes the physics you see.

Third was **friction**. Whether a domino slides or tips depends on friction, and Coulomb friction is non-smooth, so it's hard to solve exactly. Get it slightly wrong and the dominoes skate across the table instead of toppling. That small detail completely changes the visual result.

And finally it showed me something more general: the physics equations are only half the story. The other half is **engineering**: data structures, solvers, performance, and making it all robust enough that you can trust what you see. That realization pushed me toward thinking about simulation not just as math, but as a systems and programming problem. In a way it planted the seed for wanting better tools, because writing these simulators by hand, getting them correct and fast, was so painful. If the infrastructure were better, people could spend their time on the interesting physics instead of fighting the code.

So dominoes taught me humility, mostly. Something that looks like a children's toy is actually a beautiful stress test for a physics engine.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulation difficulties such as jitter, sinking, instability, and incorrect friction effects, but does not clearly state that dominoes led Hu to recognize rigid-body interaction models can be substantially inaccurate.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, that's a story that goes back quite a while, actually. When I was a kid I loved setting up dominoes, and later, when I started programming, I thought, this should be easy to simulate. It's just blocks falling over and hitting each other. How hard can it be?

It turned out to be really hard, and that was the lesson. The first thing I learned is that contact is the whole problem. Free-flying rigid bodies are almost trivial, you just integrate position and orientation. But the moment two boxes touch, you have to detect the collision, figure out the contact points and normals, and then decide what forces to apply so they don't interpenetrate. My first attempt used a naive penalty method, basically stiff springs pushing things apart. The dominoes would either jitter like crazy or explode across the screen, because the stiffness you need to keep them from sinking into each other forces you to use absurdly small time steps.

The second thing was friction. A domino doesn't just tip over, it pivots on an edge and the base has to stay put. If your friction model is sloppy, the bottom slides out and the whole chain never propagates. That taught me that Coulomb friction is non-smooth, it's an inequality constraint, and you really need something like an impulse-based or LCP-style solver that handles contact and friction together, rather than bolting them on as separate forces.

And the third thing, which maybe shaped me the most, was how sensitive the whole chain is. A domino run is a cascade. A tiny error in the first collision, maybe a slightly wrong restitution or a bit of energy injected by the solver, gets amplified down the line. Thirty dominoes in, the simulation looks nothing like reality. That gave me a lot of respect for numerical stability and energy behavior, and it made me suspicious of simulators that look fine in a single demo but drift when you chain many interactions together.

Honestly, I think that experience is part of why I later cared so much about making simulation both fast and programmable. When each experiment takes forever to run, you can't iterate on these subtle contact and friction issues. You want to try a different solver, a different time integrator, and see the dominoes fall again in seconds. So the dominoes didn't just teach me rigid-body dynamics, they taught me what I wanted the tooling to feel like.

r001.rationale: The candidate says domino simulations exposed problems with contact, friction, and numerical error, noting that small collision errors compound until the simulated chain looks nothing like reality. This communicates that rigid-body interaction models can be substantially inaccurate.

astra-6.text:
Dominoes look like a very simple system, but when you try to simulate them, you realize how much is happening. Each domino rotates, hits another domino, and stays in contact with the ground. You have to account for gravity, friction, and the impulses from those collisions—not just detect that two objects overlap.

The interesting part is that small errors can propagate through the whole chain. If the collision response or the timing is slightly wrong, the dominoes might bounce unnaturally, penetrate each other, or stop falling. So it helped me understand that rigid-body simulation is really about handling contact and constraints reliably. Writing down the equations of motion is only part of the problem; making them behave consistently on a computer is the other part.

r001.rationale: The response says small errors in collision response or timing can cause bad behavior, but it does not state that models of rigid-body interactions can be substantially inaccurate.

sol-6.1.text:
Trying to simulate dominoes made me realize how much complexity is hidden in something that looks simple. You have these rigid blocks, but the interesting behavior comes from contact: when they collide, how they push on one another, and how friction affects whether they slide or tip over. A small error in handling those interactions can change the whole chain reaction.

So it helped me understand that rigid-body simulation isn’t just about writing down Newton’s laws. You also need a numerical method that can handle collisions and contact consistently. Getting something to move is relatively easy; getting it to behave plausibly and remain stable is the challenging part.

r001.rationale: The response says small errors in handling contact interactions can change the chain reaction, but it does not state that models of rigid-body interactions can be substantially inaccurate.
